content.text: Students build from prior lessons on credibility, usefulness, relevance, and paraphrasing to review whether their selected sources and fact notes truly support their inquiry into a hidden innovator.
Research grows stronger when people carefully use evidence, ask clarifying questions, and collaborate to improve understanding.
Students will revise and expand their research notes, group evidence into categories, and begin shaping informative writing from their strongest facts.

Today’s peer review helps students strengthen the evidence base they will use to explain an innovator’s contribution, significance, and need for recognition in the final research article and presentation.

Students will evaluate and gather relevant information from multiple sources by assessing source accessibility, interest, relevance, and evidence support and by reviewing research notes with peers to improve the quality of their notes.
Students will use discourse markers, clarifying questions, and feedback stems to provide evidence-based peer critique about source use and paraphrased notes.

Turn and Talk
Directions:
In the previous lesson, you filled in your Fact column by paraphrasing and quoting key evidence. Today, you will review your notes with a partner to make them clearer and stronger.
How can feedback from a peer make your research stronger?
Language Study

In this lesson, you are practicing how to make your evidence sound citation-ready. A dropped-in quote places quotation marks in a sentence without introducing the source, so the evidence feels incomplete. Strong research writing blends the evidence into your own sentence by naming the source first. If a quote is longer than what you need, you can use an ellipsis to remove extra words while keeping the meaning clear.
According to _____,
The article _____ explains that ____
. . . (to show omitted words in a quotation)
Model and Deconstruct
Dropped-in quote: "Jackson became NASA’s first Black female engineer in 1958."
Revised sentence:
According to the article
Mary Jackson Biography
, Jackson "became NASA’s first Black female engineer in 1958."
What was added to improve the sentence?
Where is the source named?
How does the lead-in help the reader?
Directions:
I

n your journal, revise one dropped-in quote into a citation-ready sentence. Use either the author’s last name or the article title to introduce the evidence. Introduce the source using an author name or article title. If needed, shorten the quote with an ellipsis.
Why is an integrated quotation stronger than a dropped-in quotation?
Part A: Review Research with a Partner
Peer Review
Directions:
Share one source and one or two fact notes. Your partner will give one strength and one suggestion or question. Then switch roles.
Listen and respond to these questions:
Is the source accessible?
Is it relevant to the research question?
Does it include helpful features (charts, captions, etc.)?
Are notes clearly paraphrased with attribution?
After exchanging specific feedback, discuss your thoughts in response to this question:
What is one strength you notice in your partner’s source or fact notes, and what is one next step you would suggest?
Part B: Revise Notes from Feedback
Directions:
Look at the feedback you received. Choose one piece of feedback and revise at least one fact note so it is clearer, better supported, or more clearly paraphrased.
Which feedback are you using, and how will it strengthen your research notes?
Reflection
Reflect on your ability to apply feedback to revise your research notes using the Reflection routine.
How confident are you in using peer feedback to improve your sources and fact notes?
Quick Write
Directions:
Explain one piece of feedback you received and how you used it.
How did peer feedback help you improve your research today?
Use this routine to connect yesterday’s evidence work to today’s collaborative review. Keep the opening focused on the unit’s essential question and on how collaboration helps improve research.
Turn and Talk
Say these Directions:
In the previous lesson, you filled in your Fact column by paraphrasing and quoting key evidence. Today, you will review your notes with a partner to make them clearer and stronger.
Ask:
How can feedback from a peer make your research stronger?

A peer can notice if one of my notes is unclear, too close to the source, or not strongly connected to my research question. Feedback can also help me see whether my sources are accessible and relevant enough to support my final writing.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
Now that students know why peer review matters, they are ready to learn how to give feedback that is specific, respectful, and based on evidence.
Students will connect yesterday’s evidence note work to today’s collaborative research review and prepare students to use academic feedback language.

This mini-lesson teaches citation-ready conventions students can use right away as they revise their research notes. Use this routine to help students notice how writers introduce expert evidence, name the source clearly, and trim long quotations so the most important information stands out.
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1q89q-BV4B6V7Lz8BXaJKBoVRNdMpSCBf/edit?usp=drive_link&ouid=116876046531374136081&rtpof=true&sd=true
Language Study

In this lesson, we are practicing how to make our evidence sound citation-ready. A dropped-in quote places quotation marks in a sentence without introducing the source, so the evidence feels incomplete. Strong research writing blends the evidence into our own sentence by naming the source first. If a quote is longer than we need, we can use an ellipsis to remove extra words while keeping the meaning clear.
According to _____,
The article _____ explains that ____
. . . (to show omitted words in a quotation)
Model and Deconstruct
Display Dropped-in quote:
"Jackson became NASA’s first Black female engineer in 1958."
Say:
This quote gives important information, but the reader does not know who said it or why it is included.
Display Revised sentence:
According to the article
Mary Jackson Biography
, Jackson "became NASA’s first Black female engineer in 1958."
Ask:
What was added to improve the sentence?
(a lead-in that names the source)
Ask:
Where is the source named?
(at the beginning of the sentence)
Ask:
How does the lead-in help the reader?
(It tells where the information comes from and connects the quote to the writer’s sentence.)
Say these Directions:

In your journal, revise one dropped-in quote into a citation-ready sentence. Use either the author’s last name or the article title to introduce the evidence. Introduce the source using an author name or article title. If needed, shorten the quote with an ellipsis.
Ask:
Why is an integrated quotation stronger than a dropped-in quotation?

An integrated quotation is stronger because it tells the reader where the evidence came from and connects the quote to my own sentence. It also sounds more professional and helps the evidence fit clearly into my paragraph.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
Now you have a clear way to make your evidence sound stronger and more professional as you review and revise research notes with a partner.
Support students in introducing expert evidence clearly, naming a source before a quotation, and using ellipses to keep quoted language focused.
Language Focus:
Attribution phrases
Article-title and author-name lead-ins
Quotation integration
Ellipses for omitted words
Research vocabulary including attribution, integrate, ellipsis
Before Language Study (preparation step—optional)
Have students orally rehearse one source lead-in using either an author’s last name or an article title before they write.
Prompt students to say the full sentence aloud before writing so they can hear whether the quotation fits smoothly into their own syntax.
Emphasize that an ellipsis should remove only unnecessary words, not key meaning, so the evidence stays accurate.
You said "I just put the quote in"—we can say: "I integrated the quote by introducing the article title before the evidence."
You said "I cut some words out"—we can say: "I used an ellipsis to omit unnecessary words while keeping the source’s meaning clear."
According to the article "_____," _____.
[Author’s last name] explains that "_____."
I used an ellipsis because _____.
Invite students to explain in everyday language what the source is saying first, then help them turn that idea into a more formal evidence sentence.
Encourage students to compare how they introduce information in conversation or storytelling at home with how writers introduce source-based information in academic writing.
If a student drops in a quote without naming the source → Prompt: "Start your sentence with ‘According to the article . . .’ or name the author before the quotation."
If a student uses an ellipsis to remove important meaning → Prompt: "Read the original line and your shortened quote side by side. What key idea must stay so the evidence is still accurate?"
If a student writes the quote as a sentence fragment → Prompt: "Say the whole sentence aloud and add your own words before or after the quote so it sounds complete."
Student introduces a quotation with an article title or author name.
Student uses an ellipsis only to remove nonessential words and keeps the source meaning accurate.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Source Lead-Ins

Display two reusable sentence starters students can copy into their journals: “According to the article ‘_____,’” and “[Author’s last name] explains that.” Using Ellipses Accurately: Have students underline the exact words they want to keep before adding quotation marks and an ellipsis. Hearing Sentence Flow: Encourage students to read the full evidence sentence aloud to check whether the quotation fits smoothly with their own words. Written Expression: Allow students to rehearse the sentence orally with a partner before writing it. Alternative Expression: Allow students to provide an oral recording of their citation-ready sentence or use speech-to-text tools to capture it in writing.
Ready for extension

Invite students to write two versions of the same evidence sentence, one using an article title and one using an author’s last name, and compare which one sounds stronger in context. Challenge students to explain why an ellipsis improves one quotation but would weaken another.

Students learn citation-ready conventions for integrating expert evidence by naming the source with an author’s last name or article title and using ellipses to remove unnecessary words from quotations.
Teacher Tip

After peer review and revision, pause for a brief self-assessment. Have students rate their work using specific criteria (e.g., paraphrasing, source relevance, use of feedback) and record their ratings in a simple visual tracker. Then guide students to set one concrete revision goal (e.g., “I will rewrite one note using my own sentence structure and include attribution”). For multilingual learners, highlight one language focus (e.g., giving critique or explaining revision using “because”) and have students track their use of that move. This supports students in monitoring both research skills and language development over time.
Part A: Review Research with a Partner (W.6.8) (20 minutes)

Using the peer review protocol, students exchange one source and one set of fact notes, then provide targeted feedback on accessibility, interest, relevance, diversity of information formats, and paraphrase quality. Have students access their Research Notes graphic organizer and top source.
Peer Review
Say these Directions:
Share one source and one or two fact notes. Your partner will give one strength and one suggestion or question. Then switch roles.
Say:
Listen and respond to these questions:
Is the source accessible?
Is it relevant to the research question?
Does it include helpful features (charts, captions, etc.)?
Are notes clearly paraphrased with attribution?
After exchanging specific feedback, discuss your thoughts in response to this question:
Ask:
What is one strength you notice in your partner’s source or fact notes, and what is one next step you would suggest?

One strength is that your source is very relevant because it directly answers your question about the innovator’s contribution. However, one note may need stronger paraphrasing because it sounds close to the source wording, so you might rewrite it in your own sentence structure.

By the end of this section, students should be able to give specific feedback about source quality and paraphrasing. They should identify at least one strength and one area for improvement in their research work.
Students engage in structured academic conversations to evaluate sources and evidence notes and to offer constructive critique.
Language Focus:
Academic critique language
Clarifying questions
Discourse markers for feedback
Explanation language tied to source accessibility, interest, relevance, and evidence support
Students silently star one fact note they most want feedback on before sharing.
Encourage students to ground feedback in a specific source feature or fact note.
Prompt students to respond to diverse information formats by naming what a chart, timeline, or caption adds to understanding.
One strength in your source selection is ___.
One question I have is ___.
You might clarify ___ by ___.
This chart, diagram, or caption helps because ___.
If students give only praise and no critique → Prompt: “Add one question or one suggestion that could improve the work.”
If students critique without evidence → Prompt: “Point to the source, note, or text feature that made you think that.”
If students ignore diverse formats → Prompt: “Name whether the chart, diagram, caption, or timeline actually helps explain the idea.”
Student gives two pieces of specific feedback using academic discourse markers.
Student asks or answers a clarifying question tied to source quality or evidence quality.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Giving Critique
Provide a two-step sentence frame
Ex: “One strength is ___. One suggestion is ___.”
Struggling with: Clarifying Peer Ideas
Encourage the use of clarifying questions.
Ex: “One question I have is how this source helps explain ___.”
Struggling with: Focusing on Evidence
Prompt students to point to the exact note or source section before giving feedback.
Struggling with: Alternative Expression
Allow students to record oral feedback for a partner before writing a final note on paper.
Ready for extension
Ask
: Compare two of a partner’s sources and explain which one seems more accessible or more relevant for the inquiry question.
Part B: Revise Notes from Feedback (W.6.8) (10 minutes)

This section shifts students from discussion to revision. Students apply peer feedback to improve the clarity, accuracy, and originality of their notes. Emphasize that revision is where research becomes stronger and more usable for writing.
Say these Directions:
Look at the feedback you received. Choose one piece of feedback and revise at least one fact note so it is clearer, better supported, or more clearly paraphrased.
Ask:
Which feedback are you using, and how will it strengthen your research notes?

I am using the feedback that one of my notes was too close to the original wording. I will strengthen it by rewriting the sentence in my own structure and adding “According to the source,” so the evidence is clearer and does not risk plagiarism.

By the end of this section, students should revise at least one note in response to feedback and explain how the revision improved their work. They should understand how revision strengthens clarity, support, and originality.
Students convert peer feedback into clearer, better-supported evidence notes and explain how revision improved the work.
Language Focus:
Revision explanation language
Attribution stems
Feedback response language
Causal connectors including because and so
Before Revision (preparation step—optional)
Students circle one piece of feedback they will act on before revising.
Encourage students to revise one note deeply rather than many notes superficially.
Prompt students to explain the effect of the revision, not only what they changed.
I used the feedback that ___.
I revised this note by ___.
This revision made my note stronger because ___.
According to the source, ___.
If students do not know which feedback to use → Prompt: “Choose the feedback that most affects clarity, paraphrasing, or attribution.”
If students revise only one word or two → Prompt: “Rebuild the sentence structure so the note sounds fully like your own language.”
If students cannot explain why the revision matters → Prompt: “Finish the sentence ‘This makes the note stronger because ___.’”
Student revises a note based on specific feedback.
Student explains how the revision improved clarity, support, or originality.
Reflection
Reflect on your ability to apply feedback to revise your research notes using the
Reflection
routine.
How confident are you in using peer feedback to improve your sources and fact notes?
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Using Feedback Productively
Ask students to choose one feedback note and rewrite it as an action step.
Struggling with: Revision Explanation
Struggling with: Provide the sentence frame
Ex: “I changed ___ because my partner noticed ___.”
Struggling with: Paraphrasing After Critique
Encourage students to cover the source, say the idea aloud, and rebuild the note in a new structure.
Struggling with: Alternative Expression
Allow students to orally explain their revisions to a partner before writing the final reflection.
Ready for extension: Extension Focus
Invite students to revise a second note and explain which revision most improved the evidence they may later use in their argument for recognition.
Part A: Review Research with a Partner (W.6.8)
Students will share sources and fact notes, ask clarifying questions, and give evidence-based feedback on source choice and paraphrase strength.
Part B: Revise Notes from Feedback (W.6.8)
Students will revise their Research Notes and record next steps based on peer feedback about source quality, support, and clarity.
This section gives students an opportunity to reflect on how feedback improved their research. Students connect revision to stronger evidence and clearer communication.
Quick Write
Say these Directions:
Explain one piece of feedback you received and how you used it.
Ask:
How did peer feedback help you improve your research today?

Peer feedback helped me notice that one of my paraphrases sounded too close to the source. I revised the note by changing the sentence structure and adding clear attribution, which makes my evidence stronger and helps me avoid plagiarism. The feedback also showed me which source details are most useful for my final writing.
Optional Sentence Starter
One piece of feedback I received was ___. I used it by ___. This made my research stronger because ___.
Say:
When we revise our research based on feedback, we make sure the evidence we use is clear and accurate, helping us better represent important contributions that may have been overlooked.

By the end of this section, students should be able to explain how feedback improved their research notes. They should understand that strong research helps build a more complete and accurate record of people’s contributions.
Students will assess their ability to reflect on feedback received and explain one revision they will make to strengthen their research.
Students should review the feedback they received today and continue strengthening their research notes. Instruct students to take notes in their
Journal
on the following prompt:

Revise at least one additional fact note using peer feedback. Write the original idea of the note, the revision you made, and one sentence explaining how the revision improved clarity, attribution, or support.

standards.description: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources; assess the credibility of each source; and quote or paraphrase the data and conclusions of others while avoiding plagiarism and providing basic bibliographic information for sources.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.
Interpret information presented in diverse media and formats (e.g., visually, quantitatively, orally) and explain how it contributes to a topic, text, or issue under study.
Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
Conduct short research projects to answer a question, drawing on several sources and refocusing the inquiry when appropriate.

Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information and evidence, paraphrasing key ideas, building on responses, and providing useful feedback.
Engage in conversational exchanges and express ideas on familiar topics by asking and answering yes‐no and wh‐ questions and responding using simple phrases.
Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information, and paraphrasing key ideas.

Justify opinions or persuade others by providing detailed and relevant textual evidence (e.g., quoting from the text directly or referring to specific textual evidence) or relevant background knowledge, with light support.
Justify opinions by providing some textual evidence (e.g., quoting from the text) or relevant background knowledge, with substantial support.
Justify opinions or persuade others by providing relevant textual evidence (e.g., quoting from the text or referring to what the text says) or relevant background knowledge, with moderate support.
